DDCL: Deep Dual Competitive Learning:
A Differentiable End-to-End Framework
for Unsupervised Prototype-Based Representation Learning

Journal: Neural Networks
Giansalvo Cirrincione Address: Lab. LTI, Université de Picardie Jules Verne, Amiens, France Email: exin@u-picardie.fr
Abstract

A persistent structural weakness in deep clustering is the disconnect between feature learning and cluster assignment. Most architectures invoke an external clustering step, typically kk-means, to produce pseudo-labels that guide training, preventing the backbone from directly optimising for cluster quality.

This paper introduces Deep Dual Competitive Learning (DDCL), the first fully differentiable end-to-end framework for unsupervised prototype-based representation learning. The core contribution is architectural: the external kk-means is replaced by an internal Dual Competitive Layer (DCL) that generates prototypes as native differentiable outputs of the network. This single inversion makes the complete pipeline, from backbone feature extraction through prototype generation to soft cluster assignment, trainable by backpropagation through a single unified loss, with no Lloyd iterations, no pseudo-label discretisation, and no external clustering step.

To ground the framework theoretically, the paper derives an exact algebraic decomposition of the soft quantisation loss into a simplex-constrained reconstruction error and a non-negative weighted prototype variance term. This identity reveals a self-regulating mechanism built into the loss geometry: the gradient of the variance term acts as an implicit separation force that resists prototype collapse without any auxiliary objective, and leads to a global Lyapunov stability theorem for the reduced frozen-encoder system.

Six blocks of controlled experiments validate each structural prediction. The decomposition identity holds with zero violations across more than 10510^{5} training epochs; the negative feedback cycle is confirmed with Pearson r=−0.98r=-0.98; with a jointly trained backbone, DDCL outperforms its non-differentiable ablation by +65%+65\% in clustering accuracy and DeepCluster end-to-end by +122%+122\%.

Keywords: 
competitive learning , deep clustering , differentiable clustering , dual competitive layer , Lyapunov stability , prototype learning

1 Introduction

Unsupervised representation learning is a central challenge in machine learning: given a large unlabeled dataset, the goal is to learn feature representations that capture the intrinsic structure of the data without relying on manual annotations [21]. Clustering-based approaches offer a natural framework for this task, grouping similar samples together and using the resulting structure to guide feature learning [8].

Convolutional neural networks trained on large supervised datasets [22] have become the dominant paradigm for visual representation learning. Yet the requirement for labeled data is a fundamental bottleneck: annotations are expensive, domain-specific, and unavailable in many scientific settings such as genomics [23] and medical imaging. This motivates the development of unsupervised methods capable of learning rich representations from raw data alone.

1.1 Motivation: the disconnect problem

A fundamental limitation shared by many deep clustering methods is the disconnect between representation learning and cluster assignment. Methods such as DeepCluster [1], DEC [3], and Deep kk-Means [6] perform feature extraction and clustering in separate stages, preventing the two objectives from being jointly optimized through backpropagation.

In DeepCluster [1], the most prominent example of this paradigm, a CNN backbone extracts features which are then clustered by kk-means; the cluster assignments are converted to discrete pseudo-labels and used to train the backbone in a subsequent supervised step. This two-stage procedure has been shown to yield strong unsupervised representations, but its structural disconnect prevents the backbone from directly optimizing for cluster quality: it can only predict whatever labels the current kk-means iteration happens to produce.

1.2 Contribution: DDCL

This paper introduces Deep Dual Competitive Learning (DDCL), the first fully differentiable end-to-end framework for unsupervised prototype-based deep clustering. The core contribution is architectural: the external kk-means is replaced by an internal Dual Competitive Layer (DCL) [2], which feeds the transposed feature matrix to the competitive layer so that prototypes emerge as native network outputs rather than internal weight vectors. This single inversion makes the complete backbone–prototype–assignment pipeline trainable by backpropagation through a single unified loss. The theoretical analysis that follows, including the loss decomposition, collapse analysis, feedback stability, and global Lyapunov theorem, constitutes a rigorous foundation for understanding why this architectural choice works.

The main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    The DDCL framework: a unified differentiable architecture replacing external kk-means with an internal DCL module, in both batch and incremental formulations.

  2. 2.

    Loss decomposition theorem: a proof that ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V where V≥0V\geq 0 is the weighted prototype variance under the soft assignment distribution.

  3. 3.

    Gradient analysis: complete characterization of gradients with respect to assignments, prototypes, and backbone parameters, including the role of stop-gradient.

  4. 4.

    Collapse analysis: proof that ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} makes prototype collapse a first-order locally unstable saddle via the implicit separation force ∇PV=2​P​Σqn\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}}, where P∈ℝd×kP\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} is the prototype matrix, Σqn=diag⁡(qn)−qn​qn⊤∈ℝk×k\Sigma_{q_{n}}=\mathrm{diag}(q_{n})-q_{n}q_{n}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k} is the soft-assignment covariance matrix, and qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1} is the soft assignment vector of sample nn (all formally defined in Section 5); this force is absent in LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}.

  5. 5.

    Feedback stability: identification and linearized analysis of a negative feedback loop between prototype separation and assignment concentration, with explicit stability conditions.

  6. 6.

    Global Lyapunov stability: a rigorous global stability theorem for the reduced (frozen-encoder) DDCL flow, establishing that the regularized energy E⁡(P,Q)E(P,Q), where P∈ℝd×kP\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} is the prototype matrix and Q={qn}n=1NQ=\{q_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} is the collection of soft assignment vectors, is a Lyapunov function, all trajectories remain bounded, and every trajectory converges to the KKT stationary set.

  7. 7.

    Extensions: principled extension to CNNs beyond AlexNet, recurrent architectures, and Transformers.

It is important to emphasize the scope of the theoretical results. The decomposition theorem and gradient analysis are exact algebraic identities. The collapse analysis establishes a first-order local instability of the collapsed configuration under ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}, not a global convergence guarantee for the full nonconvex deep system. The feedback stability analysis is a linearized characterization of the reduced prototype–assignment dynamics, providing structural insight and a practical design rule rather than a full nonlinear convergence proof. The global Lyapunov theorem (Section 5.6) is a genuine global result, but applies to the reduced system with frozen encoder features; global asymptotic stability of the full end-to-end DDCL system remains an open problem (Section 5.7). The goal of this paper is not to establish large-scale state-of-the-art benchmark performance, but to provide the theoretical foundation and controlled validation of a differentiable prototype-based deep clustering framework. The numerical experiments in Section 7 are designed to verify these structural predictions; large-scale GPU validation on standard visual benchmarks is identified as the primary direction for future work.

1.3 Paper organization

Section 2 reviews related work. Section 3 recalls DeepCluster and DCL. Section 4 introduces the DDCL framework. Section 5 develops the theoretical analysis, culminating in the global Lyapunov stability result. Section 6 discusses architectural extensions. Section 7 presents numerical validation. Section 8 provides a practical discussion. Section 9 concludes. Proofs are collected in the Appendices.

2 Related Work

2.1 Deep clustering

Deep clustering methods [8] combine representation learning with clustering objectives. DEC [3] minimizes the KL divergence between soft assignments and a sharpened target distribution, jointly training an autoencoder and cluster centers; its improved variant IDEC [25] preserves local structure through a reconstruction term. JULE [4] alternates between agglomerative clustering and network updates in a recurrent framework. Deep Adaptive Image Clustering [5] learns mappings that bring augmented pairs close in feature space. Deep kk-Means [6] embeds kk-means directly into the network loss via a differentiable relaxation, but without a dedicated prototype generation module. Deep Subspace Clustering [7] uses self-expressive layers to capture subspace structure.

Two recent methods pursue end-to-end differentiable clustering through a different route. ClAM [34] (ICML 2023) proposes a continuous relaxation of the discrete assignment problem using Associative Memory dynamics, enabling differentiable clustering via SGD; however, it operates in the ambient data space and does not learn latent representations, limiting its applicability to high-dimensional data. DCAM [35] (NeurIPS 2024) extends this idea to latent space by using Associative Memory attractor dynamics as an inductive bias inside an autoencoder, making the encoder, decoder, and cluster prototypes jointly differentiable. DDCL differs from both in three fundamental respects: (i) prototypes are native outputs of the backbone graph via the DCL module, not latent attractors of a recurrent memory system; (ii) no decoder is required, so the framework is composable with any backbone architecture; (iii) the competitive learning formulation admits a rigorous algebraic decomposition and Lyapunov analysis that have no analogue in associative memory methods.

More recent methods exploit self-supervised pretraining. SCAN [26] decouples representation learning from clustering assignment in two explicit phases: a contrastive pretraining step followed by a neighborhood-based cluster assignment. DINO [27] shows that Vision Transformer features trained with self-distillation contain rich semantic structure directly exploitable for clustering without further training. CC [28] combines instance-level and cluster-level contrastive objectives in a single end-to-end framework. Prototypical contrastive learning (PCL, [29]) explicitly maintains cluster prototypes and uses them as additional contrastive anchors, arriving at a similar motivation to DDCL but from a contrastive rather than competitive learning perspective, and without the theoretical decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V.

The key structural difference between DDCL and all these methods is summarized as follows. SwAV [15], which combines contrastive learning with online clustering by assigning augmented views to shared prototypes, and PCL use prototypes as contrastive anchors within an augmentation-based objective: prototypes are cluster centroids maintained outside the backbone graph and updated via an EM or momentum step, not as differentiable outputs. SCAN separates pretraining from clustering in two distinct phases with no joint gradient signal. DDCL differs in three specific ways: (i) prototypes are native outputs of the backbone graph (DCL module), not external centroids; (ii) the entire system is optimized by a single unified loss ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} with continuous gradient flow; (iii) the decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V and its consequences (collapse resistance via ∇PV\nabla_{P}V, the feedback cycle, and the Lyapunov theorem) have no analogue in contrastive or EM-based prototype methods. The present paper focuses on the theoretical analysis of this integration; empirical comparison with SCAN, DINO, and PCL on large-scale visual benchmarks is left for future work.

Table 1 provides a structured comparison of DDCL against the most relevant existing methods along five dimensions: whether prototypes are native outputs of the backbone graph, whether the framework requires a reconstruction decoder, whether training uses a single differentiable loss with no alternating steps, whether data augmentation is needed, and whether a rigorous theoretical analysis of the loss geometry accompanies the method. The table covers the full spectrum from classical deep clustering (DEC, DeepCluster, Deep kk-Means) through modern self-supervised methods (SwAV, PCL) to the two most closely related differentiable clustering approaches (ClAM, DCAM).

The key observation from Table 1 is that DDCL is the only method that simultaneously satisfies all five criteria. The columns denote: Native protos — prototypes are differentiable outputs of the backbone graph, not external centroids; No decoder — no reconstruction decoder is required; Unified loss — a single differentiable objective with continuous gradient flow; No augmentation — no data augmentation or contrastive views; Theory — rigorous analysis of loss geometry and dynamics. The most discriminating column is Native protos: no prior method generates prototypes as differentiable outputs of the backbone computational graph. DEC and DeepCluster maintain cluster centres as external parameters updated outside the gradient flow. SwAV and PCL update prototypes via Sinkhorn-Knopp or EM steps that are decoupled from the backbone. ClAM and DCAM achieve differentiable clustering but through associative memory dynamics rather than competitive learning: ClAM operates only in the ambient data space without representation learning, while DCAM requires a full autoencoder and uses memory attractors as prototypes rather than native network outputs. The Theory column reflects that, unlike all of these methods, DDCL comes with a rigorous analysis: an exact loss decomposition, a characterisation of collapse resistance, a linearised feedback stability result, and a global Lyapunov theorem for the reduced system.

Self-supervised methods [9, 10] avoid explicit clustering by designing pretext tasks. More recently, contrastive methods such as SimCLR [11] and MoCo [12] learn representations by contrasting augmented views of the same image. BYOL [13] and SimSiam [14] operate without negative pairs. SwAV [15] bridges contrastive and clustering objectives (discussed in Section 2 in relation to DDCL).

2.2 Competitive learning

Competitive learning [16] is a biologically inspired paradigm where neurons compete to represent input patterns. The Self-Organizing Map (SOM) [17] organizes prototypes on a fixed low-dimensional grid, combining competition with topology preservation. Growing Neural Gas (GNG) [18] relaxes the fixed topology by incrementally adding units where the quantization error is highest. Both methods learn prototype positions through Competitive Hebbian Learning (CHL) [19], which encodes the first- and second-winner structure in a topology graph. The GH-EXIN network [20] extends these ideas to hierarchical clustering by nesting competitive layers at multiple granularity levels.

A fundamental limitation shared by all these methods is that prototypes are weight vectors internal to a single layer: they are not accessible as differentiable outputs and cannot be backpropagated through from a downstream loss. The DCL [2] resolves this by transposing the input matrix before the competitive layer, so that prototypes appear as explicit, differentiable columns of the output matrix (formally defined in Section 3.2). This architectural inversion makes prototype generation fully differentiable and composable with any downstream objective. It also enables the gradient boundedness property (DCL gradients live in the nn-dimensional data subspace regardless of dd, the feature dimension), which is central to the high-dimensional robustness of DDCL. The regression interpretation of DCL, connecting competitive learning to OLS and its variants (TLS, weighted LS), is developed in [2] and further grounded in the neural data-fitting framework of [30].

3 Background

3.1 DeepCluster

Let {xn}n=1N\{x_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} be NN unlabeled input samples. A backbone CNN fθf_{\theta} with parameters θ\theta extracts features zn=fθ​(xn)∈ℝdz_{n}=f_{\theta}(x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, collected in the feature matrix Fθ=[z1,…,zN]∈ℝd×NF_{\theta}=[z_{1},\dots,z_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N}, where dd is the feature dimension. Throughout the paper, kk denotes the number of prototypes (clusters), specified a priori.

DeepCluster [1] proceeds as follows:

  1. 1.

    Feature preprocessing: PCA to D≪dD\ll d dimensions, ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalization, whitening.

  2. 2.

    External clustering: run kk-means on {zn}\{z_{n}\} to obtain centroids C∈ℝd×kC\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k} and hard assignments yn∈{0,1}ky_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{k}, yn⊤​𝟏k=1y_{n}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{k}=1.

  3. 3.

    Pseudo-label training: train fθf_{\theta} and a linear classifier head gϕg_{\phi} (weights ϕ\phi) to predict the pseudo-labels. The classifier output is:

    s^n=softmax⁡(gϕ​(zn))∈ℝk,\hat{s}_{n}=\mathrm{softmax}(g_{\phi}(z_{n}))\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, (1)

    where s^n,j\hat{s}_{n,j} is the predicted probability of sample nn belonging to cluster jj. The cross-entropy loss is: LDC=−1N∑nlogs^n,ynL_{\mathrm{DC}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\log\hat{s}_{n,y_{n}}, where yn∈{1,…,k}y_{n}\in\{1,\dots,k\} is the integer cluster index assigned by kk-means (i.e., the component of yny_{n} that equals 1 in the one-hot encoding).

  4. 4.

    Repeat until convergence.

The kk-means step solves:

minC,{yn}⁡1N​∑n‖zn−C​yn‖2s.t.yn∈{0,1}k,yn⊤​𝟏k=1.\min_{C,\{y_{n}\}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\|z_{n}-Cy_{n}\|^{2}\quad\text{s.t.}\quad y_{n}\in\{0,1\}^{k},\;y_{n}^{\top}\mathbf{1}_{k}=1. (2)

DeepCluster includes two mechanisms to prevent trivial solutions: empty cluster reassignment and uniform cluster sampling [1].

The fundamental limitation is structural: kk-means is external to the computational graph. Gradients do not flow through the assignment step, so the backbone cannot directly optimize for cluster quality.

3.2 The Dual Competitive Layer (DCL)

The DCL was introduced in [2] as a gradient-based competitive learning module that generates prototypes as differentiable network outputs by operating on the transposed feature matrix. In what follows, X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} denotes a generic input matrix of nn samples (which in the DDCL context corresponds to the current batch, n≤Nn\leq N); dd is the feature dimension and kk the number of prototypes, as defined in Section 3. The construction and the two properties most relevant to DDCL are recalled below.

Vanilla Competitive Layer (VCL)

The VCL is the classical competitive learning unit [16, 17] as it appears in the neural network literature. Given an input matrix X∈ℝn×dX\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d} (nn samples, each with dd features, arranged as rows), a VCL with kk neurons (where kk is specified a priori and may not equal the true number of clusters in the data) has weight matrix W1∈ℝk×dW_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d}, where each row wj⊤∈ℝdw_{j}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is a prototype vector. For each sample xi∈ℝdx_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, the winning neuron is j∗=arg⁡minj⁡‖xi−wj‖2j^{*}=\arg\min_{j}\|x_{i}-w_{j}\|^{2}, and the loss is the quantization error:

Q=∑i=1nminj⁡‖xi−wj‖2.Q=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\min_{j}\|x_{i}-w_{j}\|^{2}. (3)

Prototypes are stored internally as weight vectors and are not directly accessible as network outputs; they cannot be connected to a downstream differentiable loss.

Dual Competitive Layer (DCL)

The key insight of [2] is to feed the transposed matrix X⊤∈ℝd×nX^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times n} to the competitive layer. With nn input neurons and kk output neurons, the DCL weight matrix is W2∈ℝn×kW_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}, whose jj-th column w2,j∈ℝnw_{2,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} contains the weights connecting all nn input neurons to the jj-th output neuron. The output layer activation matrix is:

P=Y2=X⊤​W2∈ℝd×k,P=Y_{2}=X^{\top}W_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, (4)

where Y2Y_{2} denotes the output activation matrix of the DCL (i.e., the result of multiplying the transposed input X⊤X^{\top} by the weight matrix W2W_{2}), whose jj-th column pj=X⊤​w2,j∈ℝdp_{j}=X^{\top}w_{2,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the jj-th prototype, expressed as a linear combination of the input data columns weighted by w2,jw_{2,j}. Prototypes are now explicit network outputs: gradients from any downstream loss flow through PP back into W2W_{2} and, via X⊤X^{\top}, into the backbone that produced XX.

The DCL loss augments the quantization error with a topology regularization term:

LDCL=Q+λ​‖E‖2,L_{\mathrm{DCL}}=Q+\lambda\|E\|^{2}, (5)

where E∈ℝk×kE\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k} is the Competitive Hebbian Learning (CHL) adjacency matrix [19], encoding the first- and second-winner co-activation structure across the training samples. Minimizing ‖E‖2\|E\|^{2} penalizes dense connectivity between prototypes, enforcing a sparse topology: only pairs of prototypes that are mutually nearest neighbours are linked, producing a graph whose connected components tend to reflect the true cluster structure of the data. This is particularly valuable in practice, since kk is set a priori and may overestimate the actual number of clusters; the sparse topology provides a visual and algorithmic means of identifying the true cluster count without rerunning the model.

Duality and equivalence

Reference [2] proves (Theorems 2.1–2.4) that VCL and DCL produce the same prototype geometry under the assumption that input samples are uncorrelated with unit variance, a condition practically achieved by batch normalization. The two architectures are therefore equivalent in representation power while DCL is strictly richer in connectivity: the same competitive dynamics, but with prototypes promoted to explicit, differentiable output tensors that participate fully in the computation graph.

Gradient subspace property

Theorems 3.4–3.5 of [2] establish that the DCL gradient ∇W2LDCL\nabla_{W_{2}}L_{\mathrm{DCL}} lies in the column space of X⊤X^{\top}, an nn-dimensional subspace of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This result has a deep practical consequence that is central to DDCL’s behavior in high-dimensional settings. In the ambient space ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, most directions are uninformative: when d≫nd\gg n, only nn linearly independent directions are spanned by the data, and the remaining d−nd-n directions contain only noise. The gradient subspace property means that DCL updates are automatically confined to the nn-dimensional data subspace, a geometric tunnel aligned with the actual information content of the batch, and completely immune to the noise that contaminates the d−nd-n orthogonal directions. This is not a regularization imposed from outside but a structural property of the dual architecture: because the prototype pj=X⊤​w2,jp_{j}=X^{\top}w_{2,j} is formed by taking a linear combination of the nn data vectors, its gradient can never escape their span. The practical effect is striking: as dd grows beyond nn, methods that operate in the full ambient space (including standard kk-means and DeepCluster) see their signal-to-noise ratio collapse, while DDCL maintains meaningful gradient updates through this subspace tunnel. Block 3 (Section 7.3) validates this property experimentally across six dimensionalities from d=10d=10 to d=5000d=5000, showing that DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) degrades gracefully at d>nd>n while all ambient-space methods converge to chance level.

4 Deep Dual Competitive Learning (DDCL)

4.1 Conceptual shift

DDCL replaces the external kk-means in DeepCluster with a DCL block. The transpose of the feature matrix Fθ∈ℝd×NF_{\theta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times N} is passed to DCL:

Fθ⊤→DCLP=[p1,…,pk]∈ℝd×k.F_{\theta}^{\top}\xrightarrow{\mathrm{DCL}}P=[p_{1},\dots,p_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}. (6)

DCL outputs the prototype matrix PP as network outputs, differentiable end-to-end. The full pipeline is:

xn→fθ→zn,Fθ⊤→DCL→P,(zn,P)→qn→ℒ.x_{n}\to f_{\theta}\to z_{n},\quad F_{\theta}^{\top}\to\mathrm{DCL}\to P,\quad(z_{n},P)\to q_{n}\to\mathcal{L}. (7)

Fig. 1 illustrates the batch DDCL pipeline with CNN backbone.

4.2 Batch DDCL with cross-entropy

The simplest DDCL variant retains the pseudo-label logic of DeepCluster. From PP, define soft assignments with temperature T>0T>0:

qn​j=exp(−∥zn−pj∥2/T)∑ℓexp(−∥zn−pℓ∥2/T),q_{nj}=\frac{\exp(-\|z_{n}-p_{j}\|^{2}/T)}{\sum_{\ell}\exp(-\|z_{n}-p_{\ell}\|^{2}/T)}, (8)

and train a linear classifier head with weight matrix Wc∈ℝk×dW_{c}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times d} and bias b∈ℝkb\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, with output probability vector

s^n=softmax⁡(Wc​zn+b)∈ℝk,\hat{s}_{n}=\mathrm{softmax}(W_{c}z_{n}+b)\in\mathbb{R}^{k}, (9)

via the soft cross-entropy loss:

LsoftCE=−1N∑n∑jqn​jlogs^n​j.L_{\mathrm{softCE}}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\sum_{j}q_{nj}\log\hat{s}_{nj}. (10)

Here s^n​j\hat{s}_{nj} is the predicted probability that sample nn belongs to cluster jj, and qn​jq_{nj} provides the soft target in place of the hard pseudo-labels used by DeepCluster.

4.3 Unified batch DDCL

In the unified formulation, the separate classifier head is eliminated. The soft quantization loss is:

ℒq=1N​∑n=1N∑j=1kqn​j​‖zn−pj‖2,\mathcal{L}_{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{k}q_{nj}\|z_{n}-p_{j}\|^{2}, (11)

with qn​jq_{nj} from (8) denoting the jj-th component of the soft assignment vector qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1}. This single loss jointly trains the backbone fθf_{\theta} and the DCL module, requiring no Lloyd iterations, no hard pseudo-labels, and no classifier head.

To prevent trivial solutions, the total loss augments ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}:

Ltot=ℒq+β​Lbal+γ​Lent+η​Lsep+λ2​‖P‖F2,L_{\mathrm{tot}}=\mathcal{L}_{q}+\beta L_{\mathrm{bal}}+\gamma L_{\mathrm{ent}}+\eta L_{\mathrm{sep}}+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|P\|_{F}^{2}, (12)

where β,γ,η,λ≥0\beta,\gamma,\eta,\lambda\geq 0 are non-negative weights, q¯=1N​∑nqn∈Δk−1\bar{q}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1} is the mean soft assignment across the batch, and:

Lbal\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{bal}} =KL(q¯∥1k𝟏k),\displaystyle=\mathrm{KL}\!\left(\bar{q}\,\Big\|\,\tfrac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}_{k}\right), (13)
Lent\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{ent}} =1N∑nH(qn),H(qn)=−∑jqn​jlogqn​j,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}H(q_{n}),\quad H(q_{n})=-\sum_{j}q_{nj}\log q_{nj}, (14)
Lsep\displaystyle L_{\mathrm{sep}} =−∑i<j∥pi−pj∥2.\displaystyle=-\sum_{i<j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|^{2}. (15)

Each term addresses a specific failure mode. LbalL_{\mathrm{bal}} is the KL divergence between the mean assignment q¯\bar{q} and the uniform distribution 1k​𝟏k\tfrac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}_{k}: minimizing it encourages all kk clusters to be used roughly equally, preventing the model from collapsing to a solution where most samples are assigned to a single prototype. LentL_{\mathrm{ent}} is the mean Shannon entropy H(qn)=−∑jqn​jlogqn​jH(q_{n})=-\sum_{j}q_{nj}\log q_{nj} of the per-sample soft assignments: maximizing it (i.e., penalizing its negative) keeps assignments soft and spread, avoiding premature hard convergence before meaningful prototype positions have been established. Lsep=−∑i<j∥pi−pj∥2L_{\mathrm{sep}}=-\sum_{i<j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|^{2} directly penalizes pairs of prototypes that are too close, providing an explicit push-apart force that complements the implicit separation already provided by ∇PV\nabla_{P}V (Section 5.4). The quadratic term λ2​‖P‖F2\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|P\|_{F}^{2} prevents prototypes from drifting to infinity under the repulsion of LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}}; its role in ensuring coercivity and hence the global Lyapunov result is discussed in Remark 1.

Remark 1 (Role of the quadratic term (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2}).

The explicit separation term LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}} is unbounded below as ‖pi−pj‖→∞\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|\to\infty, so it cannot by itself guarantee that prototype trajectories remain bounded. The quadratic regularizer (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2} (λ>0\lambda>0) introduces a restoring force towards the origin that, together with LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}}, confines the prototypes to a bounded region: LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}} pushes prototypes apart, while (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2} prevents them from drifting to infinity. This coercivity is essential for the global Lyapunov result of Section 5.6. In practice λ\lambda is chosen small (e.g. 10−410^{-4}–10−310^{-3}) so that its effect on prototype geometry is negligible.

4.4 Constrained OLS interpretation

The name LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} reflects the classical Ordinary Least Squares problem from linear regression. Given a feature vector zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} and a prototype matrix P=[p1,…,pk]∈ℝd×kP=[p_{1},\dots,p_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, the goal is to find an assignment vector qn∈ℝkq_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} such that the linear combination P​qnPq_{n} approximates znz_{n} as closely as possible. This is precisely the OLS problem minqn⁡‖zn−P​qn‖2\min_{q_{n}}\|z_{n}-Pq_{n}\|^{2}, which in unconstrained form has the closed-form solution qn=(P⊤​P)−1​P⊤​znq_{n}=(P^{\top}P)^{-1}P^{\top}z_{n}. The constraint qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1}, i.e., the entries of qnq_{n} are non-negative and sum to one, turns it into a simplex-constrained OLS problem, which no longer has a closed form but admits efficient projected-gradient solvers. Relaxing the hard one-hot constraint in (11) to the probability simplex Δk−1={q≥0:𝟏⊤​q=1}\Delta^{k-1}=\{q\geq 0:\mathbf{1}^{\top}q=1\} gives the simplex-constrained OLS loss:

LOLS=‖zn−P​qn‖2=‖zn−p¯n‖2,p¯n=P​qn.L_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\|z_{n}-Pq_{n}\|^{2}=\|z_{n}-\bar{p}_{n}\|^{2},\quad\bar{p}_{n}=Pq_{n}. (16)

Hard DDCL (T→0T\to 0) recovers a discrete one-hot OLS problem equivalent to kk-means. Soft DDCL is a continuous simplex-constrained OLS problem.

Remark 2 (Beyond OLS: noise assumptions and regression variants).

OLS assumes that observation errors lie entirely in the feature space znz_{n} (errors-in-response model). When both observations znz_{n} and prototype coordinates PP are subject to noise, Total Least Squares (TLS) provides a more appropriate formulation, minimizing orthogonal distances to the prototype subspace rather than vertical residuals. More generally, the choice of regression criterion (OLS, TLS, weighted LS, or robust variants) should be guided by the noise structure of the representation space; a systematic treatment of these regression problems and their neural implementations is given in [30].

4.5 Incremental DDCL

In the incremental formulation, prototype rows are generated sequentially: the DCL produces one row r(t)⊤∈ℝkr^{(t)\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} per step. After tt steps, the partial prototype matrix is P1:t∈ℝt×kP_{1:t}\in\mathbb{R}^{t\times k}. Defining truncated features zn,1:t∈ℝtz_{n,1:t}\in\mathbb{R}^{t}, the incremental assignment update is:

qn(t)=argminq∈Δk−1∥zn,1:t−P1:tq∥2.q_{n}^{(t)}=\arg\min_{q\in\Delta^{k-1}}\|z_{n,1:t}-P_{1:t}q\|^{2}. (17)

This is solved online via Widrow–Hoff with simplex projection:

en(t)\displaystyle e_{n}^{(t)} =zn​t−r(t)⊤​qn(t−1),\displaystyle=z_{nt}-r^{(t)\top}q_{n}^{(t-1)}, (18)
q~n(t)\displaystyle\tilde{q}_{n}^{(t)} =qn(t−1)+μ​en(t)​r(t),\displaystyle=q_{n}^{(t-1)}+\mu\,e_{n}^{(t)}r^{(t)}, (19)
qn(t)\displaystyle q_{n}^{(t)} =ΠΔk−1​(q~n(t)),\displaystyle=\Pi_{\Delta}^{k-1}\!\left(\tilde{q}_{n}^{(t)}\right), (20)

where en(t)∈ℝe_{n}^{(t)}\in\mathbb{R} is the scalar prediction error at step tt, μ>0\mu>0 is the Widrow–Hoff step size, and ΠΔk−1\Pi_{\Delta}^{k-1} is the Euclidean projection onto Δk−1\Delta^{k-1}, computed via the efficient algorithm of [2].

Simplex projection

The Euclidean projection ΠΔk−1​(v)\Pi_{\Delta}^{k-1}(v) maps any vector v∈ℝkv\in\mathbb{R}^{k} to the nearest point in the probability simplex Δk−1={q∈ℝk:q≥0, 1⊤q=1}\Delta^{k-1}=\{q\in\mathbb{R}^{k}:q\geq 0,\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}q=1\}. It can be computed exactly in O⁡(k​log⁡k)O(k\log k) time via the following sorting-based algorithm [2]:

  1. 1.

    Sort vv in descending order: v(1)≥v(2)≥⋯≥v(k)v_{(1)}\geq v_{(2)}\geq\cdots\geq v_{(k)}.

  2. 2.

    Find the largest ρ∈{1,…,k}\rho\in\{1,\dots,k\} such that v(ρ)−1ρ​(∑j=1ρv(j)−1)>0v_{(\rho)}-\frac{1}{\rho}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\rho}v_{(j)}-1\right)>0.

  3. 3.

    Set the threshold θ∗=1ρ​(∑j=1ρv(j)−1)\theta^{*}=\frac{1}{\rho}\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{\rho}v_{(j)}-1\right).

  4. 4.

    Return ΠΔk−1​(v)=max⁡(v−θ∗​𝟏k, 0)\Pi_{\Delta}^{k-1}(v)=\max(v-\theta^{*}\mathbf{1}_{k},\,0).

This operation replaces the unconstrained update q~n(t)\tilde{q}_{n}^{(t)} with the nearest feasible assignment vector, ensuring qn(t)∈Δk−1q_{n}^{(t)}\in\Delta^{k-1} at every step with no iterative inner loop. A complete pseudocode of the incremental loop is given in H. The total incremental objective is:

Linc=∑t=1dαtL(t),L(t)=1N∑n∥zn,1:t−P1:tqn(t)∥2,L_{\mathrm{inc}}=\sum_{t=1}^{d}\alpha_{t}L^{(t)},\quad L^{(t)}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n}\|z_{n,1:t}-P_{1:t}q_{n}^{(t)}\|^{2}, (21)

with non-negative weights αt\alpha_{t} typically increasing with tt.

5 Theoretical Analysis

The core theoretical results are developed below. Throughout this section a single sample zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, prototypes P=[p1,…,pk]∈ℝd×kP=[p_{1},\dots,p_{k}]\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, and a soft assignment qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1} are fixed. The notation is: p¯n=P​qn\bar{p}_{n}=Pq_{n} (prototype mixture), dn=(‖zn−p1‖2,…,‖zn−pk‖2)⊤∈ℝkd_{n}=(\|z_{n}-p_{1}\|^{2},\dots,\|z_{n}-p_{k}\|^{2})^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k} (distance vector). All proofs are in the Appendices.

5.1 Loss decomposition

Theorem 1 (Loss decomposition).

For any zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, P∈ℝd×kP\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times k}, qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1}:

ℒq=LOLS+V⁡(P,qn),\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V(P,q_{n}), (22)

where the variance term

V⁡(P,qn)=∑jqn​j​‖pj−p¯n‖2≥0V(P,q_{n})=\sum_{j}q_{nj}\|p_{j}-\bar{p}_{n}\|^{2}\geq 0 (23)

is the weighted variance of the prototypes under qnq_{n}. Equality holds iff qnq_{n} is a vertex of Δk−1\Delta^{k-1} or all active prototypes coincide.

Corollary 1 (Upper bound).

0≤V⁡(P,qn)≤14​diam​(P)20\leq V(P,q_{n})\leq\tfrac{1}{4}\mathrm{diam}(P)^{2}, where diam⁡(P)=maxi≠j⁡‖pi−pj‖\mathrm{diam}(P)=\max_{i\neq j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\| is the prototype diameter.

The decomposition (22) reveals that ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} always overestimates LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} by the prototype variance. The gap vanishes only in the hard-assignment limit and grows with prototype dispersion.

5.2 Temperature and entropic structure

Since ℒq=dn⊤​qn\mathcal{L}_{q}=d_{n}^{\top}q_{n} is linear in qnq_{n}, its unconstrained minimizer over Δk−1\Delta^{k-1} is always a vertex (hard assignment, equivalent to kk-means). Soft assignments arise solely from entropic regularization:

Proposition 1 (Entropic regularization).

The soft assignments in (8), qn​j(T)∝exp(−dn​j/T)q_{nj}(T)\propto\exp(-d_{nj}/T), are the unique minimizer of:

minqn∈Δk−1⁡{dn⊤​qn−T⋅H⁡(qn)},\min_{q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1}}\left\{d_{n}^{\top}q_{n}-T\cdot H(q_{n})\right\}, (24)

with limT→0qn​(T)=ej∗\lim_{T\to 0}q_{n}(T)=e_{j^{*}} (kk-means hard assignment, where ej∗∈{0,1}ke_{j^{*}}\in\{0,1\}^{k} is the standard basis vector for the nearest prototype j∗=arg⁡minj⁡dn​jj^{*}=\arg\min_{j}d_{nj}) and limT→∞qn​(T)=1k​𝟏k\lim_{T\to\infty}q_{n}(T)=\tfrac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}_{k} (uniform).

Corollary 2 (Monotonicity of VV).

V​(P,qn​(T))V(P,q_{n}(T)) is monotone non-decreasing in TT, with V|T→0=0V|_{T\to 0}=0 and V|T→∞=Var⁡(P)≜1k​∑j‖pj‖2−‖1k​∑jpj‖2V|_{T\to\infty}=\mathrm{Var}(P)\triangleq\tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{j}\|p_{j}\|^{2}-\|\tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{j}p_{j}\|^{2} (the unweighted prototype variance).

Temperature TT is therefore the master parameter of DDCL: it controls the softness of assignments, the magnitude of VV, the backbone learning signal, and the implicit separation force (Section 5.4).

5.3 Gradient analysis

Define the assignment covariance matrix:

Σqn=diag⁡(qn)−qn​qn⊤∈ℝk×k.\Sigma_{q_{n}}=\mathrm{diag}(q_{n})-q_{n}q_{n}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}. (25)
Proposition 2 (Gradients w.r.t. qnq_{n}).
∇qnLOLS\displaystyle\nabla_{q_{n}}L_{\mathrm{OLS}} =2​P⊤​(p¯n−zn),\displaystyle=2P^{\top}(\bar{p}_{n}-z_{n}), (26)
∇qnℒq\displaystyle\nabla_{q_{n}}\mathcal{L}_{q} =dn(constant in qn),\displaystyle=d_{n}\quad\text{(constant in $q_{n}$)}, (27)
∇qnV\displaystyle\nabla_{q_{n}}V =(‖pj‖2)j−2​P⊤​p¯n.\displaystyle=(\|p_{j}\|^{2})_{j}-2P^{\top}\bar{p}_{n}. (28)
Proposition 3 (Gradients w.r.t. PP).
∇PLOLS\displaystyle\nabla_{P}L_{\mathrm{OLS}} =2​(p¯n−zn)​qn⊤,\displaystyle=2(\bar{p}_{n}-z_{n})q_{n}^{\top}, (29)
∇Pℒq\displaystyle\nabla_{P}\mathcal{L}_{q} =2​(P−zn​𝟏k⊤)​diag​(qn),\displaystyle=2(P-z_{n}\mathbf{1}_{k}^{\top})\mathrm{diag}(q_{n}), (30)
∇PV\displaystyle\nabla_{P}V =2​P​Σqn.\displaystyle=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}}. (31)
Proposition 4 (Gradients w.r.t. znz_{n}).

Under stop-gradient on qnq_{n}:

∇znℒq|sg=∇znLOLS|sg=2​(zn−p¯n).\nabla_{z_{n}}\mathcal{L}_{q}\big|_{\mathrm{sg}}=\nabla_{z_{n}}L_{\mathrm{OLS}}\big|_{\mathrm{sg}}=2(z_{n}-\bar{p}_{n}). (32)

Under full gradient, both losses acquire a correction 𝒪⁡(T−1)\mathcal{O}(T^{-1}) proportional to Σqn\Sigma_{q_{n}}, and ∇znℒq−∇znLOLS=∇znV\nabla_{z_{n}}\mathcal{L}_{q}-\nabla_{z_{n}}L_{\mathrm{OLS}}=\nabla_{z_{n}}V.

Corollary 3 (Stop-gradient as design choice).

With stop-gradient on qnq_{n}, ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} and LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} give identical backbone updates. The difference between the two losses is felt exclusively in the DCL module gradients ∇P\nabla_{P} and the assignment gradients ∇qn\nabla_{q_{n}}. Without stop-gradient, both losses enrich the backbone signal by a term ∝T−1​Σqn\propto T^{-1}\Sigma_{q_{n}}, coupling backbone and assignment dynamics.

Properties of Σqn\Sigma_{q_{n}}: Σqn⪰0\Sigma_{q_{n}}\succeq 0; rank⁡(Σqn)≤k−1\mathrm{rank}(\Sigma_{q_{n}})\leq k-1 with qn∈ker⁡(Σqn)q_{n}\in\ker(\Sigma_{q_{n}}); tr⁡(Σqn)=1−‖qn‖2∈[0,(k−1)/k]\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q_{n}})=1-\|q_{n}\|^{2}\in[0,(k-1)/k]; Σqn→0\Sigma_{q_{n}}\to 0 as T→0T\to 0; Σqn→1k​Ik−1k2​𝟏𝟏⊤\Sigma_{q_{n}}\to\tfrac{1}{k}I_{k}-\tfrac{1}{k^{2}}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} as T→∞T\to\infty.

5.4 Prototype collapse

Prototype collapse (multiple prototypes converging to the same point) is one of the most dangerous failure modes in deep clustering.

Proposition 5 (LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}: collapse is a stable fixed point).

If pi=pj=p∗p_{i}=p_{j}=p^{*}, then ∂LOLS/∂pi\partial L_{\mathrm{OLS}}/\partial p_{i} and ∂LOLS/∂pj\partial L_{\mathrm{OLS}}/\partial p_{j} point in the same direction. No differential force acts to separate them; collapse is a stable attractor of LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}.

Proposition 6 (ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}: collapse is an unstable saddle).

Consider a perturbation pi=p∗+ε​up_{i}=p^{*}+\varepsilon u, pj=p∗−ε​up_{j}=p^{*}-\varepsilon u, ‖u‖=1\|u\|=1. Under gradient descent on ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}, the net force along uu separating pip_{i} from pjp_{j} is:

Fsep=2​ε​(qn​i+qn​j)>0,F_{\mathrm{sep}}=2\varepsilon(q_{ni}+q_{nj})>0, (33)

absent under LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} at first order. Hence collapse is an unstable saddle of ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}.

The source of this implicit separation is ∇PV=2​P​Σqn\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}}. To see why, recall from the decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V that minimizing ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} simultaneously minimizes the reconstruction error and the prototype variance VV. The gradient ∇PV=2​P​Σqn\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}} points in the direction that increases VV, so the gradient descent step on ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} pushes the prototypes in the direction that decreases VV — that is, it increases the spread of the prototype distribution. Since the assignment covariance Σqn=diag⁡(qn)−qn​qn⊤\Sigma_{q_{n}}=\mathrm{diag}(q_{n})-q_{n}q_{n}^{\top} is positive semidefinite with eigenvalues that grow when assignments are more uniform, the force P​ΣqnP\Sigma_{q_{n}} is strongest when the prototypes are close and the assignments are undecided — precisely the regime of incipient collapse. This is why ∇PV\nabla_{P}V acts as a self-regulating separation force: it is automatically largest where it is most needed.

Proposition 7 (Separation intensity vs. TT).

‖∇PV‖F=2​‖P​Σqn‖F\|\nabla_{P}V\|_{F}=2\|P\Sigma_{q_{n}}\|_{F} is monotone non-decreasing in TT, vanishing as T→0T\to 0. At T→∞T\to\infty:

‖∇PV‖F→2​‖P⁡(1k​Ik−1k2​𝟏𝟏⊤)‖F.\|\nabla_{P}V\|_{F}\to 2\left\|P\!\left(\tfrac{1}{k}I_{k}-\tfrac{1}{k^{2}}\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}\right)\right\|_{F}. (34)
Corollary 4 (Role of LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}}).

The explicit term LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}} in (15) acts as a backup mechanism, most necessary when TT is small and the implicit force ∇PV\nabla_{P}V is weak. The weight η\eta should be chosen inversely proportional to T⋅tr​(Σqn​(T))T\cdot\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q_{n}}(T)).

5.5 Negative feedback and stability

To analyze the self-regulating dynamics of DDCL, three scalar quantities that capture the essential state of the system at each training step. Intuitively, the training process involves two competing tendencies: prototypes want to separate (to cover the data better), while assignments want to sharpen (to commit to a single prototype per sample). The three quantities below make this competition precise.

The feedback quantities are defined as:

𝒮⁡(P)\displaystyle\mathcal{S}(P) =1(k2)∑i<j∥pi−pj∥2(separation),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{\binom{k}{2}}\sum_{i<j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|^{2}\quad\text{(separation)}, (35)
𝒦⁡(qn)\displaystyle\mathcal{K}(q_{n}) =∥qn∥2(concentration, ∈[1/k,1]),\displaystyle=\|q_{n}\|^{2}\quad\text{(concentration, $\in[1/k,1]$)}, (36)
ℐ⁡(Σqn)\displaystyle\mathcal{I}(\Sigma_{q_{n}}) =tr(Σqn)=1−𝒦(separation force).\displaystyle=\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{q_{n}})=1-\mathcal{K}\quad\text{(separation force)}. (37)

𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) measures how spread out the prototypes are on average: it is zero when all prototypes coincide (total collapse) and grows as they move apart. 𝒦⁡(qn)=‖qn‖2\mathcal{K}(q_{n})=\|q_{n}\|^{2} measures how concentrated the soft assignment of sample nn is: it equals 11 when qnq_{n} is a one-hot vector (hard assignment to a single prototype) and equals 1/k1/k when qn=1k​𝟏kq_{n}=\tfrac{1}{k}\mathbf{1}_{k} (maximally uncertain, uniform over all prototypes). ℐ⁡(Σqn)=1−𝒦\mathcal{I}(\Sigma_{q_{n}})=1-\mathcal{K} is the complementary measure of assignment uncertainty, and — as established by ∇PV=2​P​Σqn\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}} above — it directly controls the magnitude of the implicit separation force.

The cycle reads:

𝒮↑⇒𝒦↑⇒ℐ↓⇒‖∇PV‖F↓⇒𝒮↓.\mathcal{S}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{K}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{I}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;\|\nabla_{P}V\|_{F}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;\mathcal{S}\downarrow. (38)

This chain of implications describes a self-correcting loop, readable as follows. When prototypes are well separated (𝒮\mathcal{S} large), each sample clearly belongs to one prototype: assignments sharpen (𝒦\mathcal{K} increases). Sharp assignments mean Σqn\Sigma_{q_{n}} shrinks toward zero (ℐ\mathcal{I} falls), which weakens the implicit separation force ‖∇PV‖F\|\nabla_{P}V\|_{F}. With less force pushing prototypes apart, separation 𝒮\mathcal{S} naturally decreases — closing the loop. The same logic runs in reverse when prototypes are too close: uniform assignments maximize ℐ\mathcal{I}, which maximizes the separation force and pushes prototypes apart. The practical consequence is that the system self-corrects in both directions: it resists prototype collapse and resists excessive dispersion, without any external intervention.

Theorem 2 (Negative feedback).

The cycle is negative: it resists both collapse (𝒮→0\mathcal{S}\to 0) and excessive dispersion (𝒮→∞\mathcal{S}\to\infty), and there exists at least one equilibrium (𝒮∗,𝒦∗)(\mathcal{S}^{*},\mathcal{K}^{*}).

Linearizing around the equilibrium with perturbations (s,κ)=(𝒮−𝒮∗,𝒦−𝒦∗)(s,\kappa)=(\mathcal{S}-\mathcal{S}^{*},\mathcal{K}-\mathcal{K}^{*}) gives a 2×22\times 2 linear dynamical system. Each quantity in the cycle is expanded to first order around (𝒮∗,𝒦∗)(\mathcal{S}^{*},\mathcal{K}^{*}). The rate of change of separation s˙\dot{s} depends on two competing effects: (i) a self-damping term proportional to b⋅sb\cdot s, which captures the direct effect of the backbone pulling features toward prototypes (tending to reduce separation at rate αDCL\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}) while the backbone also spreads them (at rate αbb\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}}); and (ii) a cross-coupling term −a​κ-a\kappa capturing how an increase in assignment concentration (more committed assignments) reduces the separation force. The rate of change of concentration κ˙\dot{\kappa} is driven entirely by the change in separation +c⋅s+c\cdot s: when prototypes are farther apart, assignments sharpen (Boltzmann softmax becomes more peaked). This gives:

(s˙κ˙)=(b−ac0)⏟J​(sκ),a,c>0,b=αbb−αDCL,\begin{pmatrix}\dot{s}\\ \dot{\kappa}\end{pmatrix}=\underbrace{\begin{pmatrix}b&-a\\ c&0\end{pmatrix}}_{J}\begin{pmatrix}s\\ \kappa\end{pmatrix},\quad a,c>0,\quad b=\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}}-\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}, (39)

where αbb,αDCL\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}},\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}} are effective learning rates of backbone and DCL, respectively. The Jacobian JJ has a clear physical reading: the off-diagonal entry −a<0-a<0 encodes the inhibitory effect of sharp assignments on separation (more commitment ⇒\Rightarrow less separation force); the entry +c>0+c>0 encodes the excitatory effect of separation on sharpness (farther prototypes ⇒\Rightarrow clearer winner); the diagonal entry bb is the net self-feedback on separation, positive when the backbone dominates and negative when the DCL dominates.

Theorem 3 (Local stability).

The equilibrium is stable iff b<0b<0; oscillatory stable (spiral) iff additionally b2<4​a​cb^{2}<4ac; unstable if b>0b>0 dominates.

Corollary 5 (Practical stability condition).
αbbαDCL<1+4​‖P‖FT⋅‖∇znfθ‖F.\frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}}}{\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}}<1+\frac{4\|P\|_{F}}{T\cdot\|\nabla_{z_{n}}f_{\theta}\|_{F}}. (40)

The backbone learning rate must not exceed the DCL learning rate by too large a margin.

The qualitative message of Corollary 5 is important for practitioners. The right-hand side grows with ‖P‖F\|P\|_{F} (larger prototype spread allows a more dominant backbone) and shrinks with TT (lower temperature means sharper assignments, so the system becomes more sensitive to imbalance between αbb\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}} and αDCL\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}). In practice this means: keep the backbone learning rate no larger than the DCL learning rate, especially at low temperatures. A ratio αbb/αDCL∈[1/10,1/3]\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}}/\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}\in[1/10,1/3] is a safe starting point; the right-hand side of the inequality then provides a temperature-dependent bound that can be monitored during training. When the condition is violated, the backbone evolves too fast relative to the prototypes, the negative feedback loop breaks down, and the system can enter an unstable regime in which prototypes fail to track the evolving feature space.

The oscillatory-stable regime (when b<0b<0 and b2<4​a​cb^{2}<4ac) is worth understanding in concrete terms. The characteristic polynomial of JJ has complex conjugate roots with negative real part, which means the solution to (39) is a damped spiral: both 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) and 𝒦⁡(qn)\mathcal{K}(q_{n}) oscillate around their equilibrium values with decreasing amplitude. In practice this manifests as visible oscillations in the clustering accuracy curve during training — the accuracy rises, then dips slightly, rises again, and so on, with each swing smaller than the last. This is not a sign of instability or divergence; it is the natural signature of a system with negative feedback and inertia, analogous to a mass-spring-damper settling toward equilibrium. Recognizing this pattern allows the practitioner to distinguish healthy convergent oscillations from pathological divergence, and to avoid premature stopping or unnecessary hyperparameter tuning in response to what is, in fact, correct system behavior.

5.6 Global Lyapunov stability of the reduced DDCL flow

The feedback stability analysis of Sections 5.5 and Theorems 2–3 is local: it characterizes behavior near the equilibrium via linearization. We now establish a global stability result for the reduced system in which the encoder features are frozen.

We work with the following setup. Assume that the encoder features zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, n=1,…,Nn=1,\dots,N, are fixed. Let Q={qn}n=1NQ=\{q_{n}\}_{n=1}^{N} with each qn∈Δk−1q_{n}\in\Delta^{k-1}. Define the regularized reduced DDCL energy:

E⁡(P,Q)=∑n=1N∑j=1kqn​j​‖zn−pj‖2+β​Lbal​(Q)+γ​Lent​(Q)+η​Lsep​(P)+λ2​‖P‖F2.E(P,Q)=\sum_{n=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{k}q_{nj}\|z_{n}-p_{j}\|^{2}+\beta L_{\mathrm{bal}}(Q)+\gamma L_{\mathrm{ent}}(Q)+\eta L_{\mathrm{sep}}(P)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|P\|_{F}^{2}. (41)

The term (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2} (λ>0\lambda>0) ensures coercivity in PP. Coercivity means, intuitively, that the energy EE grows without bound whenever the prototypes drift far from the origin: E⁡(P,Q)→+∞E(P,Q)\to+\infty as ‖P‖F→∞\|P\|_{F}\to\infty. This matters because Lsep=−∑i<j∥pi−pj∥2L_{\mathrm{sep}}=-\sum_{i<j}\|p_{i}-p_{j}\|^{2} is itself unbounded below as prototypes move apart: without a counterweight, the optimization landscape would have no lower bound and trajectories could escape to infinity. The quadratic term (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2} acts as a soft barrier: it grows as ‖P‖F2\|P\|_{F}^{2}, which eventually dominates the −‖P‖F2-\|P\|_{F}^{2} growth of LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}} and pulls the energy back up. The net effect is that the combined term η​Lsep+λ2​‖P‖F2\eta L_{\mathrm{sep}}+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|P\|_{F}^{2} has a bounded minimizer: prototypes are pushed apart by LsepL_{\mathrm{sep}}, but cannot drift arbitrarily far because (λ/2)​‖P‖F2(\lambda/2)\|P\|_{F}^{2} grows faster. Every sublevel set {(P,Q):E⁡(P,Q)≤M}\{(P,Q):E(P,Q)\leq M\} is therefore compact in PP, which is the key technical condition required to invoke LaSalle’s invariance principle in the proof of Theorem 4.

The continuous-time reduced DDCL dynamics are given by the projected gradient flow:

P˙\displaystyle\dot{P} =−∇PE​(P,Q),\displaystyle=-\nabla_{P}E(P,Q), (42)
q˙n\displaystyle\dot{q}_{n} =ΠTqn​Δ​(−∇qnE​(P,Q)),\displaystyle=\Pi_{T_{q_{n}}\Delta}\!\left(-\nabla_{q_{n}}E(P,Q)\right), (43)

where Tqn​ΔT_{q_{n}}\Delta denotes the tangent cone of the simplex at qnq_{n}, and ΠTqn​Δ\Pi_{T_{q_{n}}\Delta} is the Euclidean projection onto that cone. These dynamics are the continuous-time counterpart of gradient descent on PP and projected gradient descent on the simplex-constrained assignment vectors qnq_{n}.

Theorem 4 (Global Lyapunov stability).

Assume that:

  1. 1.

    the feature vectors znz_{n} are fixed;

  2. 2.

    E⁡(P,Q)E(P,Q) is continuously differentiable;

  3. 3.

    LbalL_{\mathrm{bal}} and LentL_{\mathrm{ent}} are bounded below (both are non-negative);

  4. 4.

    λ>0\lambda>0.

Then every trajectory of the projected gradient flow (42)–(43) is bounded, the energy E⁡(P⁡(t),Q⁡(t))E(P(t),Q(t)) is non-increasing, and every trajectory converges to the set of KKT stationary points of the constrained problem.

Proof.

See F. ∎

Corollary 6 (Uniqueness implies global asymptotic stability).

If E⁡(P,Q)E(P,Q) has a unique KKT stationary point (P⋆,Q⋆)(P^{\star},Q^{\star}), then this equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable.

Interpretation.

Theorem 4 establishes a genuine global stability statement for the reduced DDCL flow:

  • 1.

    all trajectories remain bounded;

  • 2.

    the total reduced DDCL energy decreases monotonically;

  • 3.

    every trajectory converges to the set of KKT stationary points.

This does not imply convergence to a unique equilibrium, because the energy may still possess several stationary configurations due to prototype permutation symmetry, clustering degeneracies, or nonconvexity of the regularizers (Corollary 6 gives the condition under which uniqueness implies global asymptotic stability).

5.7 Limits of the global result and the full DDCL system

Theorem 4 is global, but only for the reduced system with frozen encoder features. In the full model, zn=fθ​(xn)z_{n}=f_{\theta}(x_{n}), so the backbone parameters θ\theta also evolve:

θ˙=−ε​∇θE​(θ,P,Q),P˙=−∇PE​(θ,P,Q),q˙n=ΠTqn​Δ​(−∇qnE​(θ,P,Q)).\dot{\theta}=-\varepsilon\nabla_{\theta}E(\theta,P,Q),\quad\dot{P}=-\nabla_{P}E(\theta,P,Q),\quad\dot{q}_{n}=\Pi_{T_{q_{n}}\Delta}\!\left(-\nabla_{q_{n}}E(\theta,P,Q)\right). (44)

This system is harder to analyze because: it is nonconvex in θ\theta; multiple stationary points are generally present; temperature annealing makes the dynamics non-autonomous; and the coupled backbone–prototype–assignment flow requires a two-timescale analysis. Global asymptotic stability of the full end-to-end DDCL system therefore remains an open problem.

A plausible route toward a stronger result is to assume that the backbone evolves on a slower timescale (0<ε≪10<\varepsilon\ll 1). If, for each fixed θ\theta, the fast subsystem (P,Q)(P,Q) admits a unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium (P⋆​(θ),Q⋆​(θ))(P^{\star}(\theta),Q^{\star}(\theta)), and if the reduced energy E¯​(θ)=E⁡(θ,P⋆​(θ),Q⋆​(θ))\bar{E}(\theta)=E(\theta,P^{\star}(\theta),Q^{\star}(\theta)) has a unique globally asymptotically stable minimizer, then it is in principle possible to prove that the full dynamics tracks the slow manifold (P,Q)≈(P⋆​(θ),Q⋆​(θ))(P,Q)\approx(P^{\star}(\theta),Q^{\star}(\theta)). This would require a singular perturbation or two-timescale stochastic approximation framework and is identified as the primary open theoretical question for future work.

6 Extensions

6.1 CNNs beyond AlexNet

DDCL requires only that the backbone provides zn=fθ​(xn)∈ℝdz_{n}=f_{\theta}(x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. Any CNN architecture (VGG [32], ResNet [33], DenseNet, EfficientNet, ConvNeXt) can serve as backbone, with no modification to the convolutional layers.

Attachment points

The DCL module can be attached at three natural positions. (i) After global average pooling: the pooled feature map zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is compact and translation-invariant; this is the most common choice and the one used in Block 4 (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10). (ii) After the penultimate fully connected layer: the representation is more task-adapted but higher-dimensional; useful when discriminative structure is concentrated in the final layers. (iii) After a dedicated projection head: a small MLP head (e.g., d→256→128d\to 256\to 128) can be inserted between backbone and DCL to reduce dimensionality and decouple prototype geometry from backbone feature statistics, following the practice of SimCLR [11].

Multi-scale variants

DCL blocks can be attached at multiple depths simultaneously, each receiving a different-resolution feature map and learning prototypes at a different granularity. This produces a hierarchical prototype structure without any additional supervision: coarse-scale blocks capture global cluster identity while fine-scale blocks resolve within-cluster sub-structure. The gradient subspace property (Section 3.2) ensures that all DCL blocks remain well-conditioned regardless of the feature dimensionality at each attachment point.

Practical note on batch size

Since prototypes pj=X⊤​w2,jp_{j}=X^{\top}w_{2,j} are linear combinations of the current batch, the batch size nn directly controls the expressiveness of the prototype subspace (Theorem 3.4 of [2]: gradients live in the nn-dimensional data subspace). For large CNN backbones, a batch size n≥2​kn\geq 2k is recommended to ensure that the data subspace is rich enough to represent all kk prototype directions.

6.2 Recurrent architectures

For sequential data xn=(xn​1,…,xn​Tn)x_{n}=(x_{n1},\dots,x_{nT_{n}}), a recurrent encoder (RNN, LSTM, GRU) produces a sequence summary zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} (final hidden state or pooled representation), and the DDCL pipeline applies directly. Incremental DDCL is especially natural here: DCL rows can be generated synchronously with hidden states, coupling temporal dynamics to prototype formation. Variants include sequence-level, time-step-level, and hierarchical clustering.

6.3 Transformers

Transformers provide class-token (zn∈ℝdz_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), averaged-token, or structured token embeddings. Three levels of DDCL are possible: sequence-level (one global embedding per input), token-level (treating each token as a separate sample, so DDCL organizes the internal token cloud into prototype mixtures), and layer-wise (applying DCL at multiple transformer layers to enforce hierarchical prototype organization). The compatibility of DDCL with attention-based architectures and masked modeling pretraining [24] is an especially promising research direction.

7 Numerical Validation of Theoretical Predictions

The following experiments are not intended as a competitive benchmark. The goal of the experiments is controlled validation of the derived structural predictions rather than state-of-the-art benchmark performance. They are designed specifically to verify, in controlled settings, each structural prediction derived in Section 5.

Evaluation metrics

All clustering results are reported in terms of three standard unsupervised clustering metrics. Clustering Accuracy (ACC) is computed as:

ACC=maxπ∈𝔖k1N∑n=1N[yn=π(y^n)],\mathrm{ACC}=\max_{\pi\in\mathfrak{S}_{k}}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathbf{1}\!\left[y_{n}=\pi(\hat{y}_{n})\right], (45)

where yny_{n} is the ground-truth label, y^n\hat{y}_{n} is the predicted cluster index, and the maximum is taken over all permutations π\pi of {1,…,k}\{1,\dots,k\} (solved via the Hungarian algorithm). Normalized Mutual Information (NMI) measures the mutual information between predicted and true label assignments, normalized by their geometric mean entropy; NMI ∈[0,1]\in[0,1] with 11 denoting perfect agreement. Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) measures the agreement between two clusterings corrected for chance; ARI =1=1 for perfect agreement and ARI ≈0\approx 0 for random assignments.

Experimental setup

Blocks 1–3 use pure NumPy implementations (no GPU), making every result fully reproducible on a standard CPU. Block 4 uses PyTorch with a pretrained ResNet-18 backbone for feature extraction on CIFAR-10; the prototype dynamics remain a NumPy implementation on the extracted features. Block 5 uses PyTorch end-to-end with a trainable MLP backbone. Block 6 validates the incremental DDCL formulation on streaming data with mini-batch updates. All implementations use standard numerical libraries (NumPy, PyTorch) and are described in sufficient detail for full reproducibility.

7.1 Block 1: Verification of structural properties

Setup: Three synthetic 2-D datasets (Moons, Circles, Spiral; n=300n=300, k=2k=2) and one Blobs dataset (n=400n=400, k=4k=4) are used. These datasets are deliberately chosen for their geometric simplicity: because the data live in two dimensions, every aspect of the training dynamics (prototype trajectories, assignment softness, and separation evolution) can be visualized directly, making it straightforward to verify whether the theoretical predictions hold or fail. No backbone is used; DDCL operates directly on the 2-D features, isolating the prototype dynamics from any feature-learning effects. The temperature is swept over T∈{0.1,0.5,1.0}T\in\{0.1,0.5,1.0\} to cover the near-hard (T→0T\to 0), intermediate, and near-uniform (T→∞T\to\infty) regimes, over 10 independent random initializations.

Results: The block confirms four structural predictions simultaneously.

Loss decomposition (Theorem 1): V≥0V\geq 0 holds at every epoch with zero violations across all datasets and temperatures; VV grows monotonically with TT, confirming the Monotonicity Corollary. The zero-violation result is notable: it holds without any enforcement mechanism, purely as a consequence of the algebraic identity ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V and the non-negativity of the variance (the identity 𝔼⁡[‖p‖2]−‖𝔼⁡[p]‖2≥0\mathbb{E}[\|p\|^{2}]-\|\mathbb{E}[p]\|^{2}\geq 0 holds for any probability weights and any vectors).

Collapse resistance (Propositions 5–7): Fig. 2 directly shows the key contrast between ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} and LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} across temperatures. In the left panel, ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} maintains a positive plateau of prototype separation 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) at all three temperatures, while LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} at T=1.0T=1.0 sees 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) decay to zero (both prototypes converge to the same point and all cluster structure is lost. In the right panel, the collapse rate of LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} grows with TT (reaching 100% at T=1.0T=1.0), while ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} shows zero collapses across all temperatures and all 10 runs, confirming that collapse is a stable attractor of LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} and an unstable saddle of ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}.

Negative feedback cycle (Theorem 2): corr⁡(𝒮,𝒦)=−0.67\mathrm{corr}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{K})=-0.67 (Moons, 200 epochs), confirming the negative feedback direction quantitatively; damped oscillations in ℐ⁡(Σqn)\mathcal{I}(\Sigma_{q_{n}}) are consistent with the oscillatory-stable regime predicted by Theorem 3 (the system spirals toward equilibrium rather than converging monotonically.

Temperature continuum: an optimal T∗∈[0.3,0.5]T^{*}\in[0.3,0.5] exists between the kk-means limit (T→0T\to 0) and the uniform limit (T→∞T\to\infty); on Moons (10 runs) ACC =0.847=0.847, NMI =0.382=0.382, ARI =0.479=0.479 are stable across all three temperatures, while VV grows from 0.0100.010 to 0.2060.206 without affecting accuracy (confirming that VV acts as a structural regularizer, not as a clustering objective: it can vary widely without degrading clustering performance, because what matters for accuracy is the relative geometry of the prototypes, not the absolute value of VV. Table 2 summarizes the main structural measurements across datasets and temperatures.

7.2 Block 2: Low-dimensional benchmark

Setup: The sklearn load_digits dataset is used: n=1797n=1797 images, d=64d=64 features (8×88\times 8 pixels), k=10k=10 classes [31]. Input features are preprocessed with PCA to 20 components (reducing d=64d=64 to 20 principal dimensions) followed by standardization (the same preprocessing step used internally by DeepCluster’s kk-means stage (ensuring a fair comparison. DDCL uses a direct DCL prototype module on these features with temperature annealing T(t)=T0exp(−t/τ)T(t)=T_{0}\exp(-t/\tau), T0=2T_{0}=2, Tmin=0.5T_{\min}=0.5, τ=80\tau=80. DeepCluster uses a faithful reimplementation: 3-layer MLP backbone with BatchNorm, PCA whitening + ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalization of extracted features, kk-means with ninit=20n_{\mathrm{init}}=20 and empty-cluster reassignment, uniform cluster sampling for CE training. All results are mean±\pmstd over 5 independent runs.

Exp 2.1 — Comparison: Table 3 reports results. All methods reach ACC ≈0.60\approx 0.60–0.640.64, consistent with literature on this benchmark [3, 25]. The key observations are: (i) DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) and DDCL(LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}) achieve comparable accuracy on PCA features, consistent with the theoretical prediction that backbone gradients are identical under stop-gradient and the difference between the two losses manifests primarily in collapse-resistance properties rather than in final accuracy when features are fixed; (ii) DeepCluster exhibits significantly higher variance (±0.091\pm 0.091 vs. ±0.053\pm 0.053 for DDCL), reflecting the instability of its alternating kk-means/pseudo-label cycle (a structural limitation that DDCL eliminates by design).

Exp 2.2 — Ablation. Temperature annealing (T0=2→Tmin=0.5T_{0}=2\to T_{\min}=0.5) consistently outperforms fixed TT (ACC =0.576=0.576 vs. 0.5630.563 for fixed T=0.5T=0.5), confirming the practical value of the temperature schedule derived from the entropic regularization analysis (Proposition 1). Fixed T=0.1T=0.1 and T=2.0T=2.0 both underperform, corresponding to the degenerate kk-means and uniform limits respectively. The ℒq+Lsep\mathcal{L}_{q}+L_{\mathrm{sep}} variant does not improve over ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} alone (ACC =0.549=0.549), suggesting that the implicit separation force ∇PV\nabla_{P}V is already sufficient on this dataset. Table 4 summarizes the ablation results.

Exp 2.3 — Dynamics and prototype visualization. The feedback cycle is sharply confirmed: corr⁡(𝒮,𝒦)=−0.98\mathrm{corr}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{K})=-0.98 across training. The phase portrait traces a smooth trajectory from the initial high-𝒦\mathcal{K} / low-𝒮\mathcal{S} regime toward the equilibrium predicted by Theorem 2. The variance term satisfies V≥0V\geq 0 in every epoch (zero violations). Fig. 3 shows the full training dynamics (top half) and the learned prototypes (bottom half). In the top half, the four panels show: (left to right) the loss decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V over training epochs; the feedback scatter between 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) and 𝒦⁡(qn)\mathcal{K}(q_{n}) (Pearson r=−0.98r=-0.98); the ACC curves; and the phase portrait tracing the trajectory (𝒮⁡(t),𝒦⁡(t))(\mathcal{S}(t),\mathcal{K}(t)) converging toward equilibrium. In the bottom half, the 10 learned DDCL prototypes are shown as 8×88\times 8 images with Hungarian-matched digit labels: each prototype converges to a visually distinct digit, confirming semantic coherence without any supervised signal. The dynamics measurements are collected in Table 5.

7.3 Block 3: High-dimensional validation

Setup: A MADELON-style dataset (n=100n=100, k=2k=2) is used across six dimensionalities d∈{10,50,200,500,1000,5000}d\in\{10,50,200,500,1000,5000\} with five methods: DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}), DDCL(LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}), DeepCluster, kk-means+PCA, kk-means (raw). Fig. 4 shows ACC and NMI on a log axis; Table 6 reports selected dd.

Results: At d=10d=10 all methods achieve ACC ≈1.0\approx 1.0. The first divergence appears at d=50d=50: DeepCluster and kk-means (raw) drop to ACC ≈0.70\approx 0.70 as noise begins to overwhelm the informative directions. At d=200d=200 (d>nd>n, transition) a three-way split emerges: kk-means+PCA leads (ACC =0.884±0.104=0.884\pm 0.104) via explicit noise suppression; DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) degrades gracefully (ACC =0.807±0.124=0.807\pm 0.124), confirming the DCL gradient subspace property; LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}, kk-means (raw), and DeepCluster all collapse toward chance (ACC ≈0.5\approx 0.5). At d=5000d=5000 all methods converge to chance level. Three structural findings hold across all dd: (i) DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) ≥\geq DDCL(LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}) at every dimensionality; (ii) the performance transition is anchored at d/n=1d/n=1, as predicted by DCL theory; (iii) DeepCluster and kk-means (raw) are the most fragile methods at every dd, while kk-means+PCA is strongest in the transition regime but collapses at d≫nd\gg n.

7.4 Block 4: Structural verification at scale (CIFAR-10)

Setup: Block 4 uses CIFAR-10 (N=50,000N=50{,}000, k=10k=10) with frozen ResNet-18 (d=512d=512, ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalised) to verify that structural predictions hold at large scale and in high-dimensional feature space, without backbone adaptation. All results: mean±\pmstd over 5 runs.

Results: Table 7 and Fig. 5 confirm three predictions. (1) Stop-gradient equivalence (Proposition 4): DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) and DDCL(LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}) produce identical metrics to three decimal places across all runs (the sharpest confirmation obtained across all blocks. (2) Loss decomposition: V≥0V\geq 0 at every epoch with zero violations; VV grows monotonically as temperature decreases, confirming the Monotonicity Corollary. (3) Feedback cycle: Pearson r=+0.98r=+0.98 between 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒦\mathcal{K}; the positive sign (vs. r=−0.98r=-0.98 in Block 2) reflects the frozen-encoder regime where backbone modulation is absent and both quantities grow monotonically together, consistent with Theorem 4. kk-means dominates in absolute ACC (0.6440.644) because frozen ImageNet features are already discriminative; DDCL’s advantage over kk-means requires end-to-end backbone adaptation (Block 5).

7.5 Block 5: End-to-end DDCL with trainable backbone

Setup: Block 5 tests whether the ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} advantage over LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} persists when the backbone is jointly optimised end-to-end. MNIST Digits (n=1,797n=1{,}797, d=64d=64, k=10k=10) is used with a three-layer MLP backbone (64→256→128→3264\to 256\to 128\to 32, BatchNorm+ReLU). Training: (1) 50-epoch SimCLR+AE warm-up on Gaussian-augmented views (λAE=0.5\lambda_{\mathrm{AE}}=0.5); (2) 300-epoch end-to-end joint optimisation with separation weight η\eta growing from 00 to 0.050.05 over the first 100 epochs. Comparisons: DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) vs. DDCL(LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}}) vs. kk-means+PCA (fixed-feature baseline) vs. DeepCluster e2e (same backbone). All results: mean±\pmstd over 3 runs.

Results: Table 8 and Fig. 6 show the key finding: with trainable backbone, ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} achieves ACC 0.378±0.0850.378\pm 0.085 vs. 0.229±0.0410.229\pm 0.041 for LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} (+65%+65\% relative) (the largest ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}–LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} gap across all six blocks. This contrasts sharply with Blocks 2 and 4, where frozen features yield identical results for both losses (Proposition 4). The divergence confirms the theoretical prediction: ∇PV\nabla_{P}V becomes the decisive factor precisely when backbone and prototypes co-adapt. DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) also substantially outperforms DeepCluster e2e (ACC 0.3780.378 vs. 0.1700.170, +122%+122\%), confirming that continuous gradient flow is superior to the alternating pseudo-label cycle under identical backbone and budget. kk-means+PCA retains the highest absolute ACC (0.5950.595) (expected on a small dataset where classical feature engineering dominates; the relevant comparison for DDCL remains the ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}–LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} gap under identical end-to-end conditions.

7.6 Block 6: Incremental DDCL (streaming validation)

Setup: Block 6 validates the incremental DDCL formulation (Section 4.5) on a streaming version of MNIST Digits. Data arrive in mini-batches of B=50B=50 samples in a single pass; no sample is revisited. Prototypes are updated online via a gradient step on each arriving batch, with temperature T(t)=max(T0e−t/τ,Tmin)T(t)=\max(T_{0}e^{-t/\tau},T_{\min}), T0=2T_{0}=2, τ=30\tau=30, Tmin=0.3T_{\min}=0.3. Comparisons: incremental DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) vs. MiniBatchKMeans (sklearn, same batch size) vs. batch DDCL (Block 2 reference ceiling, ACC =0.602±0.053=0.602\pm 0.053). All results: mean±\pmstd over 5 runs. Fig. 7 shows ACC and prototype separation 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) as functions of samples seen.

Results: Table 9 reports final metrics after a single streaming pass. Incremental DDCL achieves ACC =0.535±0.063=0.535\pm 0.063, within the error margin of MiniBatchKMeans (0.587±0.0770.587\pm 0.077); the difference is not statistically significant given the overlap of standard deviations. Both streaming methods fall below the batch DDCL ceiling (0.6020.602), as expected from the single-pass constraint. Fig. 7 (left) shows that incremental DDCL converges smoothly as samples accumulate, without the oscillations characteristic of hard-assignment streaming methods. Fig. 7 (right) shows that prototype separation 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) grows monotonically and stabilises, confirming that the implicit separation force ∇PV\nabla_{P}V remains active in the incremental regime.

8 Discussion

8.1 Comparison with DeepCluster

Table 10 summarizes the structural differences between DeepCluster and DDCL. Six experimental blocks add quantitative confirmation: (i) variance reduced 1.7×1.7\times (Block 2); (ii) at d/n=2d/n=2, ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} ACC =0.807=0.807 vs. DeepCluster 0.5030.503 (Block 3), with the gap growing monotonically in dd; (iii) corr⁡(𝒮,𝒦)=−0.98\mathrm{corr}(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{K})=-0.98 and −0.67-0.67 confirm the negative feedback loop that DeepCluster lacks (Blocks 1–2); (iv) ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} never collapses across all settings; LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} collapses at high TT (Block 1); (v) on CIFAR-10 frozen features (Block 4), DeepCluster achieves ACC =0.154=0.154, worst across all methods; (vi) with trainable backbone (Block 5), DDCL(ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}) outperforms DeepCluster e2e by +122%+122\% (ACC 0.3780.378 vs. 0.1700.170) and LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} by +65%+65\% (the largest ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}–LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} gap observed, confirming that ∇PV\nabla_{P}V matters most when the backbone co-adapts; (vii) in the incremental streaming regime (Block 6), the implicit separation force ∇PV\nabla_{P}V remains active in a single-pass setting, with prototype separation growing monotonically across the data stream.

8.2 Theoretical predictions vs. experimental outcomes

All five major structural predictions are confirmed across all six blocks. (1) V≥0V\geq 0 always: zero violations in >105>10^{5} epochs (Blocks 1–3), confirmed at scale in Block 4 (N=50,000N=50{,}000, d=512d=512). (2) VV monotone in TT: VV grows from 0.0100.010 to 0.2060.206 while ACC remains unchanged (Block 1 temperature sweep, Block 2 ablation); confirmed in Block 4 where VV grows monotonically as temperature decreases. (3) Collapse resistance: ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} maintains 𝒮⁡(P)>0\mathcal{S}(P)>0 at all temperatures while LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} collapses at high TT (Blocks 1 and 3). (4) Negative feedback cycle: corr(𝒮,𝒦)=−0.67(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{K})=-0.67 (Block 1), −0.98-0.98 (Block 2), +0.98+0.98 (Block 4). The sign reversal in Block 4 is theoretically coherent: the frozen-encoder regime suppresses the backbone modulation that drives self-regulating oscillations, so 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒦\mathcal{K} grow monotonically rather than forming a negative loop. (5) T→0T\to 0 gives kk-means, T→∞T\to\infty gives uniform: confirmed by the temperature ablation in Block 2.

The ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} advantage over LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} depends critically on whether the backbone is frozen or trainable: on fixed features (Blocks 2 and 4) both losses are statistically indistinguishable (Proposition 4), while with trainable backbone (Block 5) ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} outperforms LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} by +65%+65\% in ACC, confirming that ∇PV\nabla_{P}V propagates into the backbone gradient only through full end-to-end coupling.

8.3 Initialization sensitivity

Both frameworks are bootstrapping methods that must self-organize from random initialization, but their failure modes differ qualitatively. DeepCluster’s hard assignment pipeline creates a brittle feedback loop: poor initial features produce unreliable pseudo-labels, which reinforce the deficiency; the high variance ±0.091\pm 0.091 (Block 2) and near-zero NMI in Block 5 are direct empirical signatures. DDCL shifts the problem from a hard bootstrap loop to a coupled dynamical stability problem (nearly uniform assignments, premature sharpening, or excessive backbone speed (all addressed by the rate-ratio condition of Corollary 5 and the temperature schedule of Section 5.5. In summary: DDCL turns a brittle hard bootstrap into a softer and more controllable one.

8.4 Practical training guidelines

The stability conditions and experimental evidence motivate a four-phase training strategy. A complete pseudocode summary of the batch training loop is given in G.

Phase 1 — Soft warm-up: Start with high temperature T≈1T\approx 1–22 and learning-rate ratio αDCL/αbb≈3\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}}/\alpha_{\mathrm{bb}}\approx 3–1010 (satisfying Corollary 5). Optionally apply stop-gradient on assignments. Balancing (LbalL_{\mathrm{bal}}) and entropy (LentL_{\mathrm{ent}}) regularization prevent trivial imbalance.

Phase 2 — Stabilization: Reduce the learning-rate asymmetry gradually. Monitor prototype separation 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) and cluster usage. Damped oscillations in 𝒦⁡(qn)\mathcal{K}(q_{n}) and 𝒮⁡(P)\mathcal{S}(P) are expected and are not a failure mode.

Phase 3 — Sharpening: Begin temperature annealing T(t)=T0exp(−t/τ)T(t)=T_{0}\exp(-t/\tau). Remove stop-gradient once 𝒮\mathcal{S} has stabilized. The phase portrait of (𝒮,𝒦)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{K}) (Fig. 3) provides a direct visual diagnostic.

Phase 4 — Structured refinement: Reduce αDCL\alpha_{\mathrm{DCL}} to avoid overshooting equilibrium. Target T∈[0.1,0.3]T\in[0.1,0.3] and 𝒦⁡(qn)→1\mathcal{K}(q_{n})\to 1.

8.5 Open problems

Several theoretical questions remain open: (i) global asymptotic stability of the joint backbone–DCL dynamics under full (non-stop-gradient) training, including the two-timescale slow–fast extension sketched in Section 5.7; (ii) identifiability of prototype configurations under ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q}; (iii) exact relationship between ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} and maximum-likelihood estimation under a Gaussian mixture model; (iv) large-scale end-to-end GPU validation on CIFAR-10 and STL-10 with a jointly trained backbone (Block 4 addressed the frozen-encoder regime; end-to-end adaptation with AlexNet or ResNet-18 at full scale remains future work).

9 Conclusion

This paper has introduced DDCL, the first fully differentiable end-to-end framework for unsupervised prototype-based deep clustering. The central architectural contribution is the replacement of the external kk-means of DeepCluster [1] with an internal DCL module [2] whose key insight is to feed the transposed feature matrix to the competitive layer, so that prototypes become native network outputs and the complete backbone–prototype–assignment pipeline is trainable by backpropagation through a single unified loss. This resolves, by design, the structural disconnect that affects all two-stage deep clustering methods.

The theoretical analysis that grounds this framework centres on the algebraic decomposition ℒq=LOLS+V\mathcal{L}_{q}=L_{\mathrm{OLS}}+V. At first glance this is a simple identity, but it has far-reaching consequences. It reveals that the soft quantization loss carries an implicit geometric structure absent from the reconstruction objective alone: the variance term VV grows with prototype dispersion and vanishes only when assignments are hard. Its gradient ∇PV=2​P​Σqn\nabla_{P}V=2P\Sigma_{q_{n}} acts as a continuous separation force, preventing prototype collapse without any explicit penalty (a form of self-regulation that is structurally guaranteed by the loss geometry rather than engineered as an add-on. The same decomposition explains why ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} and LOLSL_{\mathrm{OLS}} appear equivalent under stop-gradient (the backbone gradient is identical for both) yet diverge dramatically when the backbone co-adapts with the prototypes: it is precisely through the extra term ∇znV\nabla_{z_{n}}V that ℒq\mathcal{L}_{q} injects richer learning signal into the backbone.

Beyond the local analysis of the negative feedback loop between prototype separation and assignment concentration, Theorem 4 establishes a genuine global result: all trajectories of the reduced frozen-encoder DDCL flow remain bounded, the regularized energy decreases monotonically along every trajectory, and convergence to the KKT stationary set is guaranteed. This provides a solid theoretical floor for the system (while honestly acknowledging that the full end-to-end stability, where the backbone itself evolves, remains an open problem requiring a two-timescale framework.

The experimental program is designed to make this theory visible.
